takeaway: Look at the whole picture, use what you have learned, and bring questions to your next clinical conversation.
why: Use pacing to make activity more repeatable while keeping the goal of doing more in view.

slides.title: Find an amount you can build on
slides.content: On a good day, it can be tempting to catch up on everything. If that repeatedly leaves you unable to do much afterwards, a steadier amount may be easier to build on.

slides.title: What pacing actually means
slides.content: You can split a task, vary what you do, take a break, or adjust the amount. The purpose is to support participation, not avoid every sensation or keep activity permanently below the same limit.

slides.title: A practical example
slides.content: Instead of completing all the household chores in one burst, someone tries a smaller block and checks how they recover. That gives them information for the next attempt. It is a learning step, not a rule that chores must always be restricted.

slides.title: Then build
slides.content: Once an amount becomes manageable, consider the next step using your response and clinical plan. There is no universal percentage to add. Start with what you can do, and build from there.

slides.title: If it was too much
slides.content: Adjust the amount next time rather than assuming the whole activity is wrong. If the response is repeatedly difficult or different from what you expected, ask for guidance.

slides.title: Try one activity
slides.content: Choose a task you want to make more consistent. Decide the amount, notice the response, and review whether to repeat or adjust it. Keep the longer-term goal in view: doing the things you enjoy.
